name: Iowa Loose Meat Sandwich

ingredients.name: neutral oil, such as vegetable or canola oil

instructions.primary_message: In a medium bowl, whisk to combine 1 tablespoon water with baking soda. Add the ground beef and mix to combine. Let sit for 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, in a small bowl, whisk the remaining 1 tablespoon water with cornstarch; set aside. In a separate small bowl, combine stock, black pepper, salt, red pepper flakes, and MSG, if using. Mix well and set aside.

In a large sauté pan or stainless-steel skillet, heat 1 tablespoon oil over high heat until shimmering. Add beef and grated onion and cook, stirring frequently and breaking the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until most of the beef is no longer pink and onions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add minced garlic and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Pour in the stock mixture and cook, stirring occasionally, until most of the liquid has evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add the cornstarch mixture and cook, stirring constantly, until the sauce has thickened and coats the ground beef, about 1 minute.

Separate the buns and place a slice of American cheese on each bottom half. Using a slotted spoon, top cheese with about 1/4 of the loose meat filling (about 4 ounces per sandwich) and press gently to compact. Top with 2 to 3 dill pickle chips and mustard. Place the top buns on, squish to compact the layers, and serve immediately.

description: This squishy, snackable Iowa loose meat sandwich brings well-seasoned beef crumbles, onion, pickles, and mustard together on a bun, for an undeniable combination of classic Midwestern flavors.
notes:
Optional or for serving: 1/4 teaspoon monosodium glutamate (MSG), optional; 4 soft burger buns, for serving (see notes); 4 slices American cheese, for serving; 8-12 dill pickle chips (the thicker-cut, the better), for serving; Brown mustard, for serving

Optional substitutions: homemade beef broth → chicken stock or store-bought low-sodium chicken broth

Notes: A potato roll is ideal, but any burger bun is fine, and using whatever you can get (within reason) is more true to the tradition than going to three stores looking for potato rolls.

Make-ahead and storage: You can make the meat ahead of time, storing it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days. We don't recommend it. The meat takes under half an hour (and minimal effort) to prep and cook combined, and it'll never be better or juicier than when it's fresh. Likewise, any leftover cooked meat can be stored in a tightly sealed container in the fridge for up to four days.
author: Jed Portman
